```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# Every number below is read from the source repository at build time: the
# verification matrix (equivalence/verification-matrix/) and the test files.
root <- normalizePath(getwd())
while (!file.exists(file.path(root, "DESCRIPTION")) && dirname(root) != root) {
  root <- dirname(root)
}
at <- function(...) file.path(root, ...)
matrix_dir <- at("equivalence", "verification-matrix")
summary <- utils::read.csv(file.path(matrix_dir, "summary.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
totals <- utils::read.csv(file.path(matrix_dir, "totals.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cells <- utils::read.csv(file.path(matrix_dir, "matrix.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
evidence <- utils::read.csv(file.path(matrix_dir, "evidence.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
evidence <- evidence[evidence$current, ]
total <- function(measure) totals$value[totals$measure == measure]
number <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
checks_of <- function(rows) sum(rows$checks[!duplicated(rows$evidence_id)])
external <- c("commercial program", "R package", "published")
by_origin <- function(origin) checks_of(evidence[evidence$origin == origin &
                                                   evidence$kind %in% external, ])
by_reference <- function(reference) checks_of(evidence[evidence$reference == reference, ])
version <- read.dcf(at("DESCRIPTION"), fields = "Version")[[1L]]

test_files <- function(dir) list.files(at(dir), "^test-.*[.]R$", full.names = TRUE)
files <- list(unit = test_files("tests/testthat"), numerical = test_files("tests/equivalence"),
              equivalence = test_files("equivalence"))
sources <- unlist(lapply(unlist(files), function(f) paste(readLines(f, warn = FALSE),
                                                           collapse = "\n")))
error_calls <- unlist(regmatches(sources, gregexpr(
  "expect_error\\((?:[^()]|\\((?:[^()]|\\([^()]*\\))*\\))*\\)", sources, perl = TRUE)))
condition_lines <- readLines(at("R", "conditions.R"), warn = FALSE)
conditions <- unique(regmatches(condition_lines, regexpr("latents_[a-z_]+", condition_lines)))
registers <- list.files(at("equivalence"), "^known-differences[.]csv$", recursive = TRUE,
                        full.names = TRUE)
register_rows <- sum(vapply(registers, function(f) nrow(utils::read.csv(f)), integer(1)))
harness_suites <- list.files(at("equivalence", "harness", "suites"), "[.]R$")
sweep_modules <- list.files(at("equivalence", "argument-sweep", "modules"), "[.]R$")
sweep_checks <- checks_of(evidence[evidence$origin == "sweep", ])
```

The numerical reliability of statistical software has been studied since
benchmark data with certified results made it measurable
(McCullough 1998; Filliben and Possolo 1999). Benchmark studies have since
assessed and compared the accuracy of widely used packages on these reference
problems (Keeling and Pavur 2007). Finite mixture models are among the
hardest cases. Their likelihood is multimodal, their class labels are not
identified, their estimates can lie on the boundary of the parameter space,
and their standard errors and selection criteria depend on conventions that
differ between programs (McLachlan and Peel 2000). When three established
programs for latent class cluster analysis were applied to a single dataset,
they returned three different solutions (Haughton, Legrand and Woolford 2009).
A user of such software has, in general, no means of telling which answer is
the correct one.

The science of computational modelling separates two questions about a
program (Oberkampf and Roy 2010). Verification asks whether the program solves
its equations correctly, that is, whether it computes the likelihood, the
estimates, the standard errors and the derived statistics that its method
defines. Validation asks whether the model, as computed, describes the system
it is meant to describe. For statistical software the second question takes a
specific form: whether estimates computed from data generated by a known
process recover that process (Cook, Gelman and Rubin 2006). latents addresses
both questions for every function it exports.

latents is developed within Dynalytics, a framework for the rigorous analysis
of the dynamics of dynamical systems (Saqr, López-Pernas and Misiejuk 2026).
Dynalytics is grounded in a scientific contract: every analytical claim must
be matched by evidence appropriate to its structure, scope and complexity.
Within Dynalytics, software is held to the same contract. Implementations
are benchmarked against established references at tight numerical tolerances
and tested on simulated data with known generating mechanisms. CarmNote, the
framework's portable, single-file analytical environment written in
JavaScript (Saqr and López-Pernas 2026), follows the same discipline: its
engines are verified against R, Python, SPSS, Mplus, NIST reference datasets
and published results, and each comparison records the reference value, the
computed value and its tolerance. This article states how the contract is met for
latents `r version` and what evidence supports it.

At this build, `r number(total("checks"))` current checks compare latents
with `r total("programs")` commercial programs, `r total("r_packages")` R
packages and `r total("papers")` published analyses on
`r number(total("datasets"))` distinct datasets, and
`r number(total("failed"))` disagree without a documented cause. Known
parameters are recovered from `r number(total("recovery_datasets"))`
simulated datasets. All `r total("functions_meeting_all")` function families
meet the four required references defined below.

# The standard of evidence

The standard adopted for latents is the strictest that the available
references allow. It rests on six principles, each of which closes a way in
which a verification record can overstate agreement.

The reference must be independent of the implementation. Agreement with code
that shares the implementation's assumptions, or its author, establishes
little. latents is therefore compared with programs written by others: the
R packages that implement the same models, and above all Mplus and Latent
GOLD, the commercial programs in which latent class, profile and transition
models are most often estimated and whose output defines practice in the
applied literature. Each function must agree with an R package, with Mplus and
with Latent GOLD. Published analyses and the output of Stata and SAS are
further sources. A program counts once, however many of its outputs are used,
and agreement on a model with a single class confirms only the arithmetic of
a regression or a density, so it is reported without counting as a source.

The criterion must be fixed before the comparison. Every tolerance is set
before the reference values are read, usually at half a unit of the last
digit the reference prints, so that the outcome cannot be adjusted to the
result. For simulation, the criteria for bias and interval coverage are fixed
before the first replicate is drawn.

The comparison must be complete. latents is compared on every quantity a
reference reports: the log likelihood, the parameter count, every estimate and
standard error, the criteria, the posteriors and the classifications. Its
arguments are varied over every option they accept. Its composite functions
are checked at each step of their composition.

A disagreement must have a cause. A difference between latents and a
reference is accepted only when it is explained by the documented behaviour of
the reference: a local maximum, a stopping rule that halts before convergence,
or a different definition of a statistic. The explanation is written in a
register beside the comparison. It expires when the difference disappears, so
that no excuse can outlive its reason, and a difference in the number of
parameters is never excused, because it indicates a different model.

Evidence must be current. Every result is saved with checksums of the package
source and of the result itself. A result counts only when both match the
present source, so a change in the code withdraws the credit of every result
obtained before it until the comparison is run again.

The evidence must be able to fail. Tests run on a machine separate from the
one on which the code is written. A skipped or erroring test earns no credit.
A failed replicate in a simulation is counted. Fits report non-convergence,
boundary estimates and failed starts as classed warnings, and inference that
the likelihood cannot support is refused.

# Layers of evidence

The evidence is organised in layers. Each layer detects a class of error that
the others cannot, and a function is considered verified when it passes all
of them.

## Layer 1. Equivalence with independent implementations

The first layer compares latents with other implementations of the same
model on the same data. `r total("r_packages")` R packages serve as references, among them
poLCA, glca, multilevLCA, depmixS4, mclust, LMest, seqHMM, flexmix and lcmm. A
harness of `r length(harness_suites)` suites runs latents and each package on
shared datasets and compares every output column
(`r number(by_origin("harness"))` current checks). Equivalence tests compare
individual models in detail, one reference per test
(`r number(by_origin("testthat"))` checks). Before every comparison the fitted
classes are matched to the reference's classes by the permutation that
minimises the distance between their parameters.

## Layer 2. The commercial reference programs

The second layer compares latents with the programs whose output defines
practice. Latent GOLD 6.1 is run on the data latents fits, and its listings
are kept with their inputs and checksums. Mplus output comes from runs of the
Mplus 9 demonstration version, from the output posted with the examples of the
Mplus User's Guide (Muthén and Muthén 1998–2017) and from the Mplus pages of
the UCLA Statistical Methods and Data Analytics group. Stata output is that of
the examples of its `gsem` manual, and SAS output that of PROC LCA, PROC FMM
and PROC TRAJ as printed in their documentation and in tutorials. A program's
conventions are reproduced before its numbers are compared. Mplus computes
robust standard errors without the small-sample factor of the sandwich
estimator, PROC LCA reports its criteria on the deviance scale, and Latent GOLD
normalises its entropy statistic by the entropy of the class sizes (Vermunt
and Magidson 2016). This layer contributes `r number(by_origin("kit"))`
checks, and its `r length(registers)` registers of explained differences hold
`r register_rows` entries in all.

```{r references}
programs <- c("Mplus", "Latent GOLD", "Stata", "SAS")
current <- cells[cells$status == "current", ]
label_of <- function(reference, kind) {
  named <- programs[vapply(programs, function(p) grepl(p, reference, fixed = TRUE), logical(1))]
  if (kind == "commercial program" && length(named) == 1L) named else
    if (kind == "published") "Published analyses" else
      if (kind == "simulation recovery") "simulab (known parameters)" else reference
}
current$source <- mapply(label_of, current$reference, current$kind)
shown <- current[current$kind %in% c(external, "simulation recovery"), ]
rows <- lapply(split(shown, shown$source), function(x) data.frame(
  Reference = x$source[[1L]], Kind = x$kind[[1L]],
  `Function families` = length(unique(x$fn)), `Current checks` = sum(x$current_checks),
  check.names = FALSE))
table <- do.call(rbind, rows)
kind_order <- c("commercial program", "R package", "published", "simulation recovery")
table <- table[order(match(table$Kind, kind_order), -table$`Current checks`), ]
table$`Current checks` <- number(table$`Current checks`)
rownames(table) <- NULL
knitr::kable(table, align = c("l", "l", "r", "r"),
             caption = "References against which latents is verified and validated.")
```

## Layer 3. Published analyses

Numbers printed in papers and books are reproduced from their data. These
include Goodman's latent class models and the worked examples published with
poLCA, mclust, LMest and lcmm. A published analysis adds a source and anchors
the comparison to a result that its authors have already defended.

## Layer 4. Recovery of known parameters

The fourth layer validates the estimates. The simulab package draws data from
latent class, latent profile, two-level, hidden Markov, regression mixture and
growth mixture models with known parameters. Each design is replicated 10 to
100 times with fixed seeds, latents is fitted to every replicate, and the
estimates are compared with the generating values. A parameter is recovered
when the mean estimate lies within 3.5 Monte Carlo standard errors of its
true value (Morris, White and Crowther 2019) and when the share of 95%
confidence intervals containing it lies within the central 99.9% binomial
range. Selection functions are judged by how often they choose the generating
number of classes, and the bootstrap likelihood-ratio test by its rejection
rates under two and three generating classes. At this build
`r number(total("recovery_checks"))` recovery checks over
`r number(total("recovery_datasets"))` simulated datasets are current.

Recovery tests methods as well as code. The three-step estimator of covariate
effects (`r3step()`, R3STEP in Mplus) produced intervals for the class
intercepts that covered the true values in 84% and 88% of replicates. The
estimator treats the classification of the first step as fixed, and its
standard errors omit that step's uncertainty (Bakk, Oberski and Vermunt 2014).
The standard errors of latents equal those of Mplus to every printed digit,
so the shortfall is a property of the method, and it is reported as one.

## Layer 5. Invariance under transformation

Equivalence on a fixed dataset cannot detect an error that two programs share,
or one that appears only in data neither program was shown. Metamorphic
testing addresses both, by applying a transformation whose effect on every
output is known in advance (Segura et al. 2016). latents is refitted after a
permutation of rows, after groups, categories and indicators are renamed,
after category order is reversed, after a change of units with scale factors
from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{6}$, after every unit is duplicated and after groups of
zero weight are added. Every output table of the refitted model must equal
the original carried through the same transformation
(`r number(by_reference("invariance"))` checks).

## Layer 6. Adversarial data and the search for the maximum

Well-behaved examples rarely expose a defect. Adversarial suites simulate the
data on which mixture software fails: a category observed in three rows,
classes that never use a category, a class of nine rows, weakly separated
classes, near-singular covariances, indicators eleven orders of magnitude
apart, more parameters than observations and likelihoods with many local
maxima. Each case separates computation from search. Started at the
reference's solution, latents must remain at that mode; started from its own
search, it must reach a maximum at least as high. Seed-stability suites refit
models under six seeds and report the spread of the maximised log likelihood.
The likelihood, its gradient and its information are rebuilt from the fitted
tables by independent code and differentiated numerically
(`r number(by_reference("numDeriv / dense likelihood") + by_reference("base-R likelihood + numDeriv"))`
checks).

## Layer 7. Refusal of invalid input

A wrong answer returned without warning is the most damaging failure of
statistical software. latents defines `r length(conditions)` classes of
condition, each documented with the input that raises it. Of the
`r number(length(error_calls))` assertions in its test suites that an input is
refused, `r number(sum(grepl("class *=", error_calls)))` require a specific
class, so a refusal for the wrong reason fails. A refusal-parity suite passes
each degenerate input through every function that accepts it and requires the
same class from each (`r number(by_reference("refusal parity"))` checks).

## Layer 8. Coverage of every argument

The layers above test each function at a few settings. The argument sweep
fits every function at each option of each argument, on several datasets, and
checks every combination against a reference that does not use the likelihood
code of latents: another package, the likelihood rebuilt from the result
tables, or a closed form. It contains `r length(sweep_modules)` modules and
`r number(sweep_checks)` current checks, and a check that cannot be attributed
to a function and a reference stops it.

## Layer 9. Composite functions

Class enumeration (`enumerate_lca()`, `enumerate_lpa()`,
`enumerate_classes()`, `compare_models()`) and the pooling of multiply imputed
analyses (`pool_imputations()`) estimate no model of their own. They fit core
models and add a layer of computation. Each is verified at every step of its
composition. An identity test requires every fit inside it to equal the direct
fit of the core function exactly, so that the evidence for the core function
applies. The added computation is compared with independent implementations:
the information criteria and classification statistics with Latent GOLD,
Mplus, mclust and poLCA, and Rubin's rules with mice, mitools and mitml. The
purpose of the function is validated by recovery.

# Coverage by function

The table gives, for each function, the number of datasets on which each
required reference agrees with latents, the number of independent sources and
the current checks. Composite functions meet the R, Mplus and Latent GOLD
requirements through their core functions.

```{r coverage}
cell <- function(key) {
  datasets <- summary[[paste0(key, "_datasets")]]
  # Recovery is never met through core functions: it has no _via_core column.
  via <- summary[[paste0(key, "_via_core")]] %||% rep(FALSE, nrow(summary))
  ifelse(!summary[[paste0("has_", key)]], "no",
         ifelse(via, sprintf("via core fits (%s)", number(datasets)),
                ifelse(datasets > 0L, number(datasets), "yes")))
}
coverage <- data.frame(
  Function = sprintf("`%s`", summary$label),
  R = cell("r"), Mplus = cell("mplus"), `Latent GOLD` = cell("latentgold"),
  `simulab recovery` = cell("recovery"), Sources = summary$n_sources,
  Checks = number(summary$checks_current), Failed = summary$failed_current,
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(coverage, align = c("l", rep("r", 7L)),
             caption = "Required references by function: datasets on which each agrees.")
```

Datasets are counted once per function. Across functions there are
`r number(total("datasets"))` distinct datasets and
`r number(total("recovery_datasets"))` simulated datasets from
`r total("recovery_designs")` simulation designs and seed sets. The
`r number(total("internal_checks"))` checks of independent code, invariance
and refusal are reported separately and do not count as sources.

# Scope

The verification covers every exported function that estimates a model or
computes a statistic from one. Plots, printed summaries and argument handling
are covered by the unit tests in `tests/testthat/`
(`r length(files$unit)` files), which check their structure and their
refusals. The comparisons with Mplus, Latent GOLD, Stata and SAS run from
listings kept in the source repository, outside the checks of the package on
CRAN, so the package depends on none of these programs.

# Documented divergences

A divergence between latents and a reference is reported with its cause and
its treatment.

| Reference | Divergence | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Mplus | MLR standard errors omit the small-sample factor $n/(n-1)$ of the sandwich estimator | latents' robust errors are scaled by $\sqrt{(n-1)/n}$ before comparison |
| Mplus | TECH11 builds its null model by deleting the first class and weights the statistic differently | likelihood-ratio statistics are compared; p-values are not |
| Mplus, Stata | local maxima at some numbers of classes | registered with the higher maximum latents reaches |
| Latent GOLD | Entropy R² is $1 - EN/(n\,H)$, with $H$ the entropy of the class sizes; latents and Mplus report $1 - EN/(n \log K)$ | the entropy $EN$ is compared, and Latent GOLD's statistic is rebuilt by its definition |
| SAS PROC LCA | EM stops when no parameter changes by more than $10^{-6}$, short of the maximum on flat likelihoods | an EM with the same rule reproduces every printed estimate to its fourth decimal |
| SAS PROC LCA | criteria are reported on the deviance scale | reproduced from latents' log likelihood |
| SAS PROC TRAJ | printed standard errors carry an undocumented factor $\sqrt{N/(N-q)}$ | measured to every printed digit and applied |
| SAS PROC FMM | equal-variance grids stop at lower maxima | registered with the higher maxima |
| flexmix | the Gaussian M-step divides by $n$ minus the rank, so its fixed point is not the maximum likelihood estimate | the step is replaced in the comparison |
| R3STEP, in latents and Mplus | intervals for class intercepts treat the first step as fixed | reported as a property of the method |
| lcmm 2.2.2 | returns no subject-specific predictions | comparisons use lcmm 2.2.1 |
| latents | `parameter_inference(boundary = "fix")` held nothing in transition fits, which were refused when a probability lay on its bound | homogeneous transition fits now hold it; their conditional standard errors agree with a numerical Hessian of the likelihood over the free coordinates; general transition fits still refuse |
